entries.d50a982854ad8ff12fb9b188c3098b2e4ac4282e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv104"/><title type="x-ms">Haggai</title> <div sID="gen20712" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20713" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">The</hi> captivity in Babylon gave a very remarkable turn to the affairs of the Jewish church both in history and prophecy. It is made a signal epocha in our Saviour's genealogy, <reference osisRef="Matt.1.17">Matt. i. 17</reference>. Nine of the twelve minor prophets, whose oracles we have been hitherto consulting, lived and preached before that captivity, and most of them had an eye to it in their prophecies, foretelling it as the just punishment of Jerusalem's wickedness. But the last three (in whom the Spirit of prophecy took its period, until it revived in Christ's forerunner) lived and preached after the return out of captivity, not immediately upon it, but some time after. Haggai and Zechariah appeared much about the same time, eighteen years after the return, when the building of the temple was both retarded by its enemies and neglected by its friends. <hi type="italic">Then the prophets, Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied unto the Jews that were in Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel, even unto them</hi> (so we read <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.1">Ezra v. 1</reference>), to reprove them for their remissness, and to encourage them to revive that good work when it had stood still for some time, and to go on with it vigorously, notwithstanding the opposition they met with in it. Haggai began two months before Zechariah, who was raised up to second him, that out of the mouth of two witnesses the word might be established. But Zechariah continued longer at the work; for all Haggai's prophecies that are recorded were delivered within four months, in the second year of Darius, between the beginning of the sixth month and the end of the ninth. But we have Zechariah's prophecies dated above two years after, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.1">Zech. vii. 1</reference>. Some have the honour to lead, others to last, in the work of God. The Jews ascribe to these two prophets the honour of being members of the great synagogue (as they call it), which was formed after the return out of captivity; we think it more certain, and it was their honour, and a much greater honour, that they prophesied of Christ. Haggai spoke of him as the <hi type="italic">glory of the latter house,</hi> and Zechariah as <hi type="italic">the man, the branch.</hi> In them the light of that morning star shone more brightly than in the foregoing prophecies, as they lived nearer the time of the rising of the Sun of righteousness, and now began to see his day approaching. The LXX. makes Haggai and Zechariah to be the penmen of <reference osisRef="Ps.146.1-Ps.148.14">Ps. cxlvi., cxlvii., and cxlviii.</reference> <div eID="gen20713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20714" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20715" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, after the preamble of the prophecy, we have, I. A reproof of the people of the Jews for their dilatoriness and slothfulness in building the temple, which had provoked God to contend with them by the judgment of famine and scarcity, with an exhortation to them to resume that good work and to prosecute it in good earnest, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. The good success of this sermon, appearing in the people's return and close application to that work, wherein the prophet, in God's name, animated and encouraged them, assuring them that God was with them, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.12-Hab.1.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv104"/> <div eID="gen20715" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20714" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Jews Reproved; God's Controversy with the Jews; The Prophet's Good Advice. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  520.)</title> <div sID="gen20716" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus speaketh the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, saying, This people say, The time is not come, the time that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house should be built. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by Haggai the prophet, saying, <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house <hi type="italic">lie</hi> waste? <hi type="super">5</hi> Now therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Consider your ways. <hi type="super">6</hi> Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages <hi type="italic">to put it</hi> into a bag with holes. <hi type="super">7</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Consider your ways. <hi type="super">8</hi> Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> Ye looked for much, and, lo, <hi type="italic">it came</hi> to little; and when ye brought <hi type="italic">it</hi> home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. Because of mine house that <hi type="italic">is</hi> waste, and ye run every man unto his own house. <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore the heaven over you is stayed from dew, and the earth is stayed <hi type="italic">from</hi> her fruit. <hi type="super">11</hi> And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon <hi type="italic">that</hi> which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon cattle, and upon all the labour of the hands. <div eID="gen20716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20717" type="x-p"/> It was the complaint of the Jews in Babylon that they <hi type="italic">saw not their signs,</hi> and there was <hi type="italic">no more prophet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Ps. lxxiv. 9</reference>), which was a just judgment upon them for mocking and misusing the prophets. We read of no prophets they had in their return, as they had in their coming out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.13">Hos. xii. 13</reference>. God stirred them up immediately by his Spirit to exert themselves in that escape (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5">Ezra i. 5</reference>); for, though God makes use of prophets, he needs them not, he can do his work without them. But the lamp of Old-Testament prophecy shall yet make some bright and glorious efforts before it expire; and Haggai is the first that appears under the character of a special messenger from heaven, when the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> had been long <hi type="italic">precious</hi> (as when prophecy began, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1 Sam. iii. 1</reference>) and <hi type="italic">there had been no open vision.</hi> In the reign of Darius Hystaspes, the third of the Persian kings, in the second year of his reign, this prophet was sent; and the word of the Lord came to him, and came by him to the leading men among the Jews, who are here named, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">v. 1</reference>. The chief governor, 1. In the state; that was <hi type="italic">Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel,</hi> of the house of David, who was commander-in-chief of the Jews, in their return out of captivity. 2. In the church; and that was <hi type="italic">Joshua the son of Josedech,</hi> who was now <hi type="italic">high priest.</hi> They were great men and good men, and yet were to be stirred up to their duty when they grew remiss. What the people also were faulty in they must be told of, that they might use their power and interest for the mending of it. The prophets, who were extraordinary messengers, did not go about to set aside the ordinary institutions of magistracy and ministry, but endeavoured to render both more effectual for the ends to which they were appointed, for both ought to be supported. Now observe, <div eID="gen20717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20718" type="x-p"/> I. What the sin of the Jews was at this time, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.2">v. 2</reference>. As soon as they came up out of captivity they set up an altar for sacrifice, and within a year after laid the foundations of a temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10">Ezra iii. 10</reference>. They then seemed very forward in it, and it was likely enough that the work would be done suddenly; but, being served with a prohibition some time after from the Persian court, and charged not to go on with it, they not only yielded to the force, when they were actually under it, which might be excused, but afterwards, when the violence of the opposition had abated, they continued very indifferent to it, had no spirit nor courage to set about it again, but seemed glad that they had a pretence to let it stand still. Though those who are employed for God may be driven off from their work by a storm, yet they must return to it as soon as the storm is over. These Jews did not do so, but continued loitering until they were afresh reminded of their duty. And that which they suggested one to another was, <hi type="italic">The time has not come, the time that the Lord's house should be built;</hi> that is, 1. "Our time has not come for the doing of it, because we have not yet recovered, after our captivity; our losses are not repaired, nor have we yet got before-hand in the world. It is too great an undertaking for new beginners in the world, as we are; let us first get our own houses up, before we talk of building churches, and in the mean time let a bare altar serve us, as it did our father Abraham." They did not say that they would not build a temple at all, but, "Not yet; it is all in good time." Note, Many a good work is put by by being put off, as Felix put off the prosecution of his convictions to a more convenient season. They do not say that they will never repent, and reform, and be religious, but, "Not yet." And so the great business we were sent into the world to do is not done, under pretence that it is all in good time to go about it. 2. "God's time has not come for the doing of it; for (say they) the restraint laid upon us by authority in a legal way is not broken off, and therefore we ought not to proceed, though there be a present connivance of authority." Note, There is an aptness in us to misinterpret providential discouragements in our duty, as if they amounted to a discharge from our duty, when they are only intended for the trial and exercise of our courage and faith. It is bad to neglect our duty, but it is worse to vouch Providence for the patronising of our neglects. <div eID="gen20718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20719" type="x-p"/> II. What the judgments of God were by which they were punished for this neglect, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">v. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9-Hag.1.11">9-11</reference>. They neglected the building of God's house, and put that off, that they might have time and money for their secular affairs. They desired to be excused from such an expensive piece of work under this pretence, that they must provide for their families; their children must have meat and portions too, and, until they have got before-hand in the world, they cannot think of rebuilding the temple. Now, that the punishment might answer to the sin, God by his providence kept them still behind-hand, and that poverty which they thought to prevent by not building the temple God brought upon them for not building it. They were sensible of the smart of the judgment, and every one complained of the unseasonable weather, the great losses they sustained in their corn and cattle, and the decay of trade; but they were not sensible of the cause of the judgment, and the ground of God's controversy with them. They did not, or would not, see and own that it was for their putting off the building of the temple that they lay under these manifest tokens of God's displeasure; and therefore God here gives them notice that this is that for which he contended with them. Note, We need the help of God's prophets and ministers to expound to us, not only the judgments of God's mouth, but the judgments of his hands, that we may understand his mind and meaning in his rod as well as in his word, to discover to us not only wherein we have offended God, but wherein God shows himself offended at us. Let us observe, <div eID="gen20719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20720" type="x-p"/> 1. How God contended with them. He did not send them into captivity again, nor bring a foreign enemy upon them, as they deserved, but took the correcting of them into his own hands; for his mercies are great. (1.) He that <hi type="italic">gives seed to the sower</hi> denied his blessing upon the <hi type="italic">seed sown,</hi> and then it never prospered; they had nothing, or next to nothing, from it. <hi type="italic">They sowed much</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">v. 6</reference>), kept a great deal of ground in tillage, which, they might expect, would turn to a better advantage than usual, because their land had long <hi type="italic">lain fallow</hi> and had <hi type="italic">enjoyed its sabbaths.</hi> Having sown much, they looked for much from it, enough to spend and enough to spare too; but they were disappointed: <hi type="italic">They bring in little,</hi> very little (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">v. 6</reference>); when they have made the utmost of it, <hi type="italic">it comes to little</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">v. 9</reference>); it did not yield as they expected. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.10">Isa. v. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">The seed of a homer shall yield an ephah,</hi> a bushel's sowing shall yield a peck. Note, Our expectations from the creature are often most frustrated when they are most raised; and then, when we look for much, it comes to little, that our expectation may be from God only, in whom it will be outdone. We are here told how they came to be disappointed (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The heaven over you is stayed from dew;</hi> he that has the key of the clouds in his hands shut them up, and withheld the rain when the ground called for it, the former or the latter rain, and then of course <hi type="italic">the earth is stayed from her fruit;</hi> for, if the heaven be as brass, the earth is as iron. The corn perhaps came up very well, and promised a very plentiful crop, but, for want of the dews at earing-time, it never filled, but was parched with the heat of the sun and withered away. The restored captives, who had long been kept bare in Babylon, thought they should never want when they had got their own land in possession again and had that at command. But what the better are they for it, unless they had the clouds at command too? God will make us sensible of our necessary and constant dependence upon him, throughout all the links in the chain of second causes, from first to last; so that we can at no time say, "Now we have no further occasion for God and his providence." See <reference osisRef="Hos.2.21">Hos. ii. 21</reference>. But God not only withheld the cooling rains, but he appointed the scorching heats (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">I called for a drought upon the land,</hi> ordered the weather to be extremely hot, and then the fruits of the earth were burnt up. See how every creature is that to us which God makes it to be, either comfortable or afflictive, serving us or incommoding us. Nothing among the inferior creatures is so necessary and beneficial to the world as the heat of the sun; it is that which puts life into the plants and <hi type="italic">renews the face of the earth at</hi> spring. And yet, if that go into an extreme, it undoes all again. Our Creator is our best friend; but, if we make him our enemy, we make the best friends we have among the creatures our enemies too. This drought God called for, and it came at the call; as the winds and the waves, so the rays of the sun, obey him. It was universal, and the ill effects of it were general; it was a drought <hi type="italic">upon the mountains,</hi> which, lying high, were first affected with it. The mountains were their pasture-grounds, and used to be <hi type="italic">covered over with flocks,</hi> but now there was no grass for them. It was <hi type="italic">upon the corn, the new wine, and the oil;</hi> all failed through the extremity of the hot weather, even <hi type="italic">all that the ground brought forth;</hi> it all withered. Nay, it had a bad influence upon men; the hot weather enfeebled some, and made them weary and faint, and spent their spirits; it inflamed others, and put them into fevers. It should seem, it brought diseases upon cattle too. In short, it spoiled <hi type="italic">all the labour of their hands,</hi> which they hoped to eat of and maintain their families by. Note, Meat for the belly is meat that perishes, and, if we labour for that only, we are in danger of losing our labour; but we are sure <hi type="italic">our labour shall not be in vain in the Lord</hi> if we labour for <hi type="italic">the meat which endures to eternal life.</hi> For the <hi type="italic">hand of the diligent,</hi> in the business of religion, will infallibly <hi type="italic">make rich,</hi> whereas, in the business of this life, the most solicitous and the most industrious often lose the labour of their hands. <hi type="italic">The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.</hi> (2.) He that gives <hi type="italic">bread to the eater</hi> denied his blessing upon the bread they ate, and then that did not nourish them. The cause of the withering and failing of the corn in the field was visible—it was for want of rain; but, besides that, there was a secret blast and curse attending that which they brought home. [1.] When they had it in the barn they were not sure of it: <hi type="italic">I did blow upon it, saith the Lord of hosts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">v. 9</reference>), and that withered it, as buds are sometimes blasted in the spring by a nipping frost, which we see the effects of, but know not the way of. <hi type="italic">I did blow it away;</hi> so the margin reads it. When men have heaped wealth together God can scatter it with the breath of his mouth as easily as we can blow away a feather. Note, We can never be sure of any thing in this world; it is exposed, not only when it is in the field, but when it is housed; for there <hi type="italic">moth and rust corrupt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.19">Matt. vi. 19</reference>. And, if we would have the comfort and continuance of our temporal enjoyments, we must make God our friend; for, if he bless them to us, they are blessings indeed, but if he blow upon them we can expect no good from them: they <hi type="italic">make themselves wings and fly away.</hi> [2.] When they had it upon the board it was not that to them that they expected: "<hi type="italic">You eat, but you have not enough,</hi> either because the meat is washy, and not satisfying, or because the stomach is greedy, and not satisfied. You eat, but you have no good digestion, and so are not nourished by it, nor does it answer the end, or you have not enough because you are not content, nor think it enough. <hi type="italic">You drink,</hi> but are not cooled and refreshed by it; <hi type="italic">you are not filled with drink;</hi> you are stinted, and have not enough to quench your thirst. The <hi type="italic">new wine is cut off from your mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.5">Joel i. 5</reference>), nay, and you <hi type="italic">drink your water</hi> too by <hi type="italic">measure and with astonishment;</hi> you have no comfort of it, because you have no plenty of it, but are still in fear of falling short." [3.] That which they had upon their backs did them no good there: "<hi type="italic">You clothe yourselves, but there is none warm;</hi> your clothes soon wear out, and wax old, and grow thin, because God blows upon them," contrary to what Israel's did in the wilderness when God blessed them. It is God that <hi type="italic">makes our garments warm upon</hi> us, when he <hi type="italic">quiets the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.37.17">Job xxxvii. 17</reference>. [4.] That which they had in their bags, which was not laid out, but laid up, they were not sure of: "<hi type="italic">He that earns wages</hi> by hard labour, and has it paid him in ready current money, <hi type="italic">puts it into a bag with holes;</hi> it drops through, and wastes away insensibly. Every thing is so scarce and dear that they spend their money as fast as they get it." Those that lay up their treasure on earth put it into a bag with holes; they lose it as they go along, and those that come after them pick it up. But, if we lay up our treasure in heaven, we provide for ourselves <hi type="italic">bags that wax not old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.33">Luke xii. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen20720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20721" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe wherefore God thus contended with them, and stopped the current of the favours promised them at their return (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.24">Joel ii. 24</reference>); they provoked him to do it: <hi type="italic">It is because of my house that is waste.</hi> This is the quarrel God has with them. The foundation of the temple is laid, but the building does not go on. "Every man <hi type="italic">runs to his own house,</hi> to finish that, and to make that convenient and fine, and no care is taken about the Lord's house; and therefore it is that God crosses you thus in all your affairs, to testify his displeasure against you for that neglect, and to bring you to a sense of your sin and folly." Note, As those who seek first the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof shall not only find them, but are most likely to have other things added to them, so those who neglect and postpone those things will not only lose them, but will justly have other things taken away from them. And if God cross us in our temporal affairs, and we meet with trouble and disappointment, we shall find this is the cause of it, the work we have to do for God and our own souls is left undone, and we <hi type="italic">seek our own things more than the things of Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.21">Phil. ii. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen20721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20722" type="x-p"/> III. The reproof which the prophet gives them for their neglect of the temple-work (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Is it time for you, O you! to dwell in your ceiled houses,</hi> to have them beautified and adorned, and your families settled in them?" They were not content with walls and roofs for necessity, but they must have for gaiety and fancy. "It is high time," says one, "that my house were wainscoted." "It is high time," says another, "that mine were painted." And God's house, all this time, <hi type="italic">lies waste,</hi> and nothing is done at it. "What!" says the prophet, "is it time that you should have your humour pleased, and not time you should have your God pleased?" How much was their disposition the reverse of David's, who could not be easy in his <hi type="italic">house of cedar</hi> while the <hi type="italic">ark of God</hi> was <hi type="italic">in curtains</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2 Sam. vii. 2</reference>), and of Solomon's, who built the temple of God before he built a palace for himself. Note, Those are very much strangers to their own interest who prefer the conveniences and ornaments of the temporal life before the absolute necessities of the spiritual life, who are full of care to enrich their own houses, while God's temple in their hearts lies waste, and nothing is done for it or in it. <div eID="gen20722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20723" type="x-p"/> IV. The good counsel which the prophet gives to those who thus despised God, and whom God was therefore justly displeased with. 1. He would have them reflect: <hi type="italic">Now therefore consider your ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.5">v. 5</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Hag.1.7">v. 7</reference>. "Be sensible of the hand of God gone out against you, and enquire into the reason; think what you have done that has provoked God thus to break in upon your comforts; and think what you will do to testify your repentance, that God may return in mercy to you." Note, It is the great concern of every one of us to consider our ways, to <hi type="italic">set our hearts to our ways</hi> (so the word is), to <hi type="italic">think on our ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.59">Ps. cxix. 59</reference>), to <hi type="italic">search</hi> and <hi type="italic">try</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.40">Lam. iii. 40</reference>), to <hi type="italic">ponder the path of our feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">Prov. iv. 26</reference>), to apply our minds with all seriousness to the great and necessary duty of self-examination, and communing with our own hearts concerning our spiritual state, our sins that are past, and our duty for the future; for sin is what we must answer for, duty is what we must do; about these therefore we must be inquisitive, rather than about events, which we must leave to God. Many are quick-sighted to pry into other people's ways who are very careless of their own; whereas our concern is to <hi type="italic">prove every one his own work,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.4">Gal. vi. 4</reference>. 2. He would have them reform (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Go up to the mountain,</hi> to Lebanon, <hi type="italic">and bring wood,</hi> and other materials that are wanting, <hi type="italic">and build the house</hi> with all speed; put it off no longer, but set to it in good earnest." Note, Our considering our ways must issue in the amending of whatever we find amiss in them. If any duty has been long neglected, that is not a reason why it should still be so, but why now at length it should be revived; better late than never. For their encouragement to apply in good earnest to this work, he assures them, (1.) That they should be accepted of him in it: <hi type="italic">Build the house, and I will take pleasure in it;</hi> and that was encouragement enough for them to apply to it with alacrity and resolution, and to go through with it, whatever it cost them. Note, Whatever God will take pleasure in, when it is done, we ought to take pleasure in the doing of, and to reckon that inducement enough to set about it, and go on with it in good earnest; for what greater satisfaction can we have in our own bosoms than in contributing any thing towards that which God will take pleasure in? It ought to be the top of our ambition to be <hi type="italic">accepted of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.9">2 Cor. v. 9</reference>. Though they had foolishly neglected the house of God, yet, if at length they will resume the care of it, God will not remember against them their former neglects, but will take pleasure in the work of their hands. Those who have long deferred their return to God, if at length they return with all their heart, must not despair of his favour. (2.) That he would be honoured by them in it: <hi type="italic">I will be glorified, saith the Lord.</hi> He will be served and worshipped in the temple when it is built, and sanctified in those that come nigh to him. It is worth while to bestow all possible care, and pains, and cost, upon that by which God may be glorified.
entries.6c08ce162398232c41dedb69e368c8745fee73fd: <div eID="gen20723" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The People's Obedience. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20724" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God had sent him, and the people did fear before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">13</hi> Then spake Haggai the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's messenger in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's message unto the people, saying, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> with you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and did work in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, their God, <hi type="super">15</hi> In the four and twentieth day of the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king. <div eID="gen20724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20725" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">As an ear-ring of gold</hi> (says Solomon), and <hi type="italic">an ornament of fine gold, so</hi> amiable, so acceptable, in the sight of God and man, <hi type="italic">is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.12">Prov. xxv. 12</reference>. The prophet here was a wise but faithful reprover, in God's name, and he met with an obedient ear. The foregoing sermon met with the desired success among the people, and their obedience met with due encouragement from God. Observe, <div eID="gen20725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20726" type="x-p"/> I. How the people returned to God in a way of duty. All those to whom that sermon was preached received the word in the love of it, and were wrought upon by it. Zerubbabel, the chief governor, did not think himself above the check and command of God's word. He was a man that had been eminently useful in his day, and serviceable to the interest of the church, yet did not plead his former merits in answer to this reproof for his present remissness, but submitted to it. Joshua's business, as high priest, was to teach, and yet he was willing himself to be taught, and willingly received admonition and instruction. <hi type="italic">The remnant of the people</hi> (and the whole body of them was but a remnant, a very few of the many thousands of Israel) also were very pliable; they all <hi type="italic">obeyed the voice of the Lord their God,</hi> and bowed their neck to the yoke of his commands, and it is here recorded to their honour that they did so, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.12">v. 12</reference>. Their father said, <hi type="italic">Sons, go work to-day in my vineyard,</hi> in my temple; and they not only said, <hi type="italic">We go, sir,</hi> but they went immediately. 1. They looked upon the prophet to be the Lord's messenger, and the word he delivered to be the Lord's message to them; and there-fore received it <hi type="italic">not as the word of man, but as the word of</hi> Almighty God; they obeyed his words, <hi type="italic">as the Lord their God had sent him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.12">v. 12</reference>. Note, In attending to God's ministers we must have an eye to him that sent them, and receive them for his sake, while they act according to their commission. 2. They <hi type="italic">did fear before the Lord.</hi> Prophecy was a new thing with them; they had had no special messenger from heaven for a great while, and therefore now that they had one, and but one, they paid an extraordinary regard to him; whereas their fathers, who had many prophets, mocked and misused them. It is sometimes so; when good preaching is most scarce it does most good, whereas the manna that is rained in plenty is loathed as <hi type="italic">light bread.</hi> And, because they so readily received this prophet, God, within a month or two after, raised them up another, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zech. i. 1</reference>. They <hi type="italic">feared before the Lord;</hi> they had a great regard to the divine authority and a great dread of the divine wrath, and were of those that <hi type="italic">trembled at God's word.</hi> The judgments of God which they had been under, though very severe, had not prevailed to make them fear before the Lord, until the word of God was sent to expound his providences, and then they feared. Note, A holy fear of God will have a great influence upon our obedience to him. <hi type="italic">Serve the Lord with fear;</hi> if we fear him not, we shall not serve him. 3. <hi type="italic">The Lord stirred up</hi> their spirits, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.14">v. 14</reference>. (1.) He excited them to their duty, and put it into their hearts to go about it. Note, Then the word of God has its success when God by his grace stirs up our spirits to comply with it; and without that grace we should remain stupid and utterly averse to every thing that is good. It is in the day of a divine power that we are made willing. (2.) He encouraged them in their duty, and with those encouragements enlarged their hearts, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Ps. cxix. 32</reference>. When they heard the word they feared; but, lest they should sink under the weight of that fear, God stirred them up, and made them cheerful and bold to encounter the difficulties they might meet with. Note, When God has work to do, he will either find or make men fit to do it, and stir them up to it. 4. They applied to their work with all possible vigour: <hi type="italic">They came and did work in the house of the Lord of hosts their God.</hi> Every one, according as his capacity or ability was, lent a hand, some way or other, to further that good work; and this they did with an eye to God as the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> and as their God, the God of Israel. The consideration of God's sovereign dominion in the world by his providence, and his covenant-relation to his people by his grace, should stir up our spirits to act for him, and for the advancement of the interest of his kingdom among men, to the utmost of our power. 5. They did this speedily; it was but on the first day of the sixth month that Haggai preached them this sermon, and by the twenty-fourth of the same month, little more than three weeks after, they were all busy working in the house of the Lord their God, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.15">v. 15</reference>. To show that they were ashamed of their delays hitherto, now that they were convinced and called they were resolved to delay no longer, but to strike while the iron was hot, and to set about the work while they were under convictions. Note, Those that have lost time have need to redeem time; and the longer we have loitered in that which is good the more haste we should make when we are convinced of our folly. <div eID="gen20726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20727" type="x-p"/> II. How God met them in a way of mercy. The same prophet that brought them the reproof brought them a very comforting encouraging word (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then spoke Haggai, the Lord's messenger, in the Lord's message,</hi> in his name, and as from him, <hi type="italic">saying, I am with you, saith the Lord.</hi> That is all he has to say, and that is enough; as that word of Christ to his disciples is (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the world. I am with you,</hi> that is, I will forgive your neglects hitherto, and they shall not be remembered against you; I will remove the judgments you have been under for those neglects, and will appear for you, as I have in them appeared against you. <hi type="italic">I am with you</hi> to protect you against your enemies that bear ill-will to your work, and to prosper you, and to give you success in it—with you to strengthen your hands, and bless the work of them, without which blessing those labour in vain that build." Note, Those that work for God have God with them; and, if he be for us, who can be against us? If he be with us, what difficulty can stand before us?  <chapter eID="Hag.1"/> <div eID="gen20727" type="x-p"/>

entries.886922f8b0ca78b6cb5a6f2e7d3409ea42edd677: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12975"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen24323" type="x-p"/> The name Haggai means "my feast"; given, according to Cocceius, in anticipation of the joyous return from exile. He probably was one of the Jewish exiles (of the tribes Judah, Benjamin, and Levi) who returned under Zerubbabel, the civil head of the people, and Joshua, the high priest, 536 B.C., when Cyrus (actuated by the striking prophecies as to himself, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Is 44:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">45:1</reference>) granted them their liberty, and furnished them with the necessaries for restoring the temple (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.23">2Ch 36:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1">Ezr 1:1</reference>; 2:2). The work of rebuilding went on under Cyrus and his successor Cambyses (called Ahasuerus in <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.6">Ezr 4:6</reference>) in spite of opposition from the Samaritans, who, when their offers of help were declined, began to try to hinder it. These at last obtained an interdict from the usurper Smerdis the Magian (called Artaxerxes in <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.7-Ezra.4.23">Ezr 4:7-23</reference>), whose suspicions were easy to rouse. The Jews thereupon became so indifferent to the work that when Darius came to the throne (521 B.C.), virtually setting aside the prohibitions of the usurper, instead of recommencing their labors, they pretended that as the prophecy of the seventy years applied to the temple as well as to the captivity in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.2">Hag 1:2</reference>), they were only in the sixty-eighth year of it [Henderson]; so that, the proper time not having yet arrived, they might devote themselves to building splendid mansions for themselves. Haggai and Zechariah were commissioned by Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag 1:1</reference>) in the second year of Darius (Hystaspes), 520 B.C., sixteen years after the return under Zerubbabel, to rouse them from their selfishness to resume the work which for fourteen years had been suspended. Haggai preceded Zechariah in the work by two months.<div eID="gen24323" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24322" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24324" type="x-p"/> The dates of his four distinct prophecies are accurately given: (1) The first (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.1-Hag.1.15">Hag 1:1-15</reference>), on the first day of the sixth month of the second year of Darius, 520 B.C., reproved the people for their apathy in allowing the temple to lie in ruins and reminded them of their ill success in everything because of their not honoring God as to His house. The result was that twenty-four days afterwards they commenced building under Zerubbabel (Hag 1:12-15). (2) The second, on the twenty-first day of the seventh month (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.1-Hag.2.9">Hag 2:1-9</reference>), predicts that the glory of the new temple would be greater than that of Solomon's, so that the people need not be discouraged by the inferiority in outward splendor of the new, as compared with the old temple, which had so moved to tears the elders who had remembered the old (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.13">13</reference>). Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel had implied the same prediction, whence some had doubted whether they ought to proceed with a building so inferior to the former one; but Haggai shows wherein the superior glory was to consist, namely, in the presence of Him who is the "desire of all nations" (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag 2:7</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>) The third, on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.10-Hag.2.19">Hag 2:10-19</reference>), refers to a period when building materials had been collected, and the workmen had begun to put them together, from which time forth God promises His blessing; it begins with removing their past error as to the efficacy of mere outward observances to cleanse from the taint of disobedience as to the temple building. (4) The fourth (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.20-Hag.2.23">Hag 2:20-23</reference>), on the same day as the preceding, was addressed to Zerubbabel, as the representative of the theocratic people, and as having asked as to the national revolutions spoken of in the second prophecy (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag 2:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24325" type="x-p"/> The prophecies are all so brief as to suggest the supposition that they are only a summary of the original discourses. The space occupied is but three months from the first to the last.<div eID="gen24325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24326" type="x-p"/> The Jews' adversaries, on the resumption of the work under Zerubbabel, Haggai, and Zechariah, tried to set Darius against it; but that monarch confirmed Cyrus' decree and ordered all help to be given to the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.3">Ezr 5:3</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.1">Ezr 6:1</reference>, &c.). So the temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius' reign 516-515 B.C. (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.14">Ezr 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen24326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24327" type="x-p"/> The style of Haggai is consonant with his messages: pathetic in exhortation, vehement in reproofs, elevated in contemplating the glorious future. The repetition of the same phrases (for example, "saith the Lord," or "the Lord of hosts," <reference osisRef="Hag.1.2">Hag 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">5, 7</reference>; and thrice in one verse, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.4">Hag 2:4</reference>; so "the spirit," thrice in one verse, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.14">Hag 1:14</reference>) gives a simple earnestness to his style, calculated to awaken the solemn attention of the people, and to awaken them from their apathy, to which also the interrogatory form, often adopted, especially tends. Chaldaisms occur (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.3">Hag 2:3</reference>; 2:6; 2:16), as might have been expected in a writer who was so long in Chaldea. Parts are purely prose history; the rest is somewhat rhythmical, and observant of poetic parallelism.<div eID="gen24327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24328" type="x-p"/> Haggai is referred to in <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.1">Ezr 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.14">6:14</reference>; and in the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">He 12:26</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, 7, 22).<div eID="gen24328" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hag.1.1-Hag.1.15">Hag 1:1-15</reference>. Haggai Calls the People to Consider Their Ways in Neglecting to Build God's House: The Evil of This Neglect to Themselves: The Honor to God of Attending to It: The People's Penitent Obedience under Zerubbabel Followed by God's Gracious Assurance.</title> <div sID="gen24329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12975"/><hi type="bold">1. second year of Darius--</hi>Hystaspes, the king of Medo-Persia, the second of the world empires, Babylon having been overthrown by the Persian Cyrus. The Jews having no king of their own, dated by the reign of the world kings to whom they were subject. Darius was a common name of the Persian kings, as Pharaoh of those of Egypt, and Cæsar of those of Rome. The name in the cuneiform inscriptions at Persepolis is written Daryawus, from the root Darh, "to preserve," the Conservator [Lassen]. Herodotus [6.98] explains it Coercer. Often opposite attributes are assigned to the same god; in which light the Persians viewed their king. <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.24">Ezr 4:24</reference> harmonizes with Haggai in making this year the date of the resumption of the building.<div eID="gen24329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sixth month--</hi>of the Hebrew year, not of Darius' reign (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.1.7">Zec 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.1">7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.3">3</reference>; 8:19). Two months later ("the eighth month," <reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zec 1:1</reference>) Zechariah began to prophesy, seconding Haggai.<div eID="gen24330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>Hebrew, Jehovah: God's covenant title, implying His unchangeableness, the guarantee of His faithfulness in keeping His promises to His people.<div eID="gen24331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by Haggai--</hi>Hebrew, "in the hand of Haggai"; God being the real speaker, His prophet but the instrument (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.7.35">Ac 7:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>).<div eID="gen24332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zerubbabel--</hi>called also Shesh-bazzar in <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.8">Ezr 1:8</reference>; 5:14, 16, where the same work is attributed to Shesh-bazzar that in <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8">Ezr 3:8</reference> is attributed to Zerubbabel. Shesh-bazzar is probably his Chaldean name; as Belteshazzar was that of Daniel. Zerubbabel, his Hebrew name, means "one born in Babylon."<div eID="gen24333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Shealtiel--</hi>or Salathiel. But <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.17">1Ch 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.19">19</reference> makes Pedaiah his father. Probably he was adopted by his uncle Salathiel, or Shealtiel, at the death of his father (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.1.12">Mt 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.27">Lu 3:27</reference>).<div eID="gen24334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">governor of Judah--</hi>to which office Cyrus had appointed him. The Hebrew Pechah is akin to the original of the modern Turkish Pasha; one ruling a region of the Persian empire of less extent than that under a satrap.<div eID="gen24335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joshua--</hi>called Jeshua (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.2">Ezr 2:2</reference>); so the son of Nun in <reference osisRef="Neh.8.17">Ne 8:17</reference>.<div eID="gen24336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Josedech--</hi>or Jehozadak (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.15">1Ch 6:15</reference>), one of those carried captive by Nebuchadnezzar. Haggai addresses the civil and the religious representatives of the people, so as to have them as his associates in giving God's commands; thus priest, prophet, and ruler jointly testify in God's name. <div eID="gen24337" type="x-p"/>
entries.697d0ecd9d5833ab3dd2b4d7e8566072caef8efa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12976"/><div sID="gen24338" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12976"/><hi type="bold">2. the Lord of hosts--</hi>Jehovah, Lord of the powers of heaven and earth, and therefore requiring implicit obedience.<div eID="gen24338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This people--</hi>"This" sluggish and selfish "people." He does not say, My people, since they had neglected the service of God.<div eID="gen24339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The time--</hi>the proper time for building the temple. Two out of the seventy predicted years of captivity (dating from the destruction of the temple, 558 B.C., <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.9">2Ki 25:9</reference>) were yet unexpired; this they make their plea for delay [Henderson]. The seventy years of captivity were completed long ago in the first year of Cyrus, 536 B.C. (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">Jr 29:10</reference>); dating from 606 B.C., Jehoiakim's captivity (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2Ch 36:6</reference>). The seventy years to the completion of the temple (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jr 25:12</reference>) were completed this very year, the second of Darius [Vatablus]. Ingenious in excuses, they pretended that the interruption in the work caused by their enemies proved it was not yet the proper time; whereas their real motive was selfish dislike of the trouble, expense, and danger from enemies. "God," say they, "hath interposed many difficulties to punish our rash haste" [Calvin]. Smerdis' interdict was no longer in force, now that Darius the rightful king was on the throne; therefore they had no real excuse for not beginning at once to build. Auberlen denies that by "Artaxerxes" in <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.7-Ezra.4.22">Ezr 4:7-22</reference> is meant Smerdis. Whether Smerdis or Artaxerxes Longimanus be meant, the interdict referred only to the rebuilding of the city, which the Persian kings feared might, if rebuilt, cause them trouble to subdue; not to the rebuilding of the temple. But the Jews were easily turned aside from the work. Spiritually, like the Jews, men do not say they will never be religious, but, It is not time yet. So the great work of life is left undone. <div eID="gen24340" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d03b4f0c6a8874e06fd96e487caeb563bd0af4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12977"/><div sID="gen24341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12977"/><hi type="bold">4. Is it time--</hi>It is not time (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.2">Hag 1:2</reference>), ye say, to build Jehovah's house; yet how is it that ye make it a fit time not only to build, but to "dwell" at ease in your own houses?<div eID="gen24341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">you, O ye--</hi>rather, for "you, you"; the repetition marking the shameful contrast between their concern for themselves, and their unconcern for God [Maurer]. Compare a similar repetition in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.24">1Sa 25:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">Zec 7:5</reference>.<div eID="gen24342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ceiled--</hi>rather, "wainscoted," or "paneled," referring to the walls as well as the ceilings; furnished not only with comfort but luxury, in sad contrast to God's house not merely unadorned, but the very walls not raised above the foundations. How different David's feelings (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2Sa 7:2</reference>)! <div eID="gen24343" type="x-p"/>
entries.c672b44aa4d0a5a066bb26fb20117a20bf2d4d5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12978"/><div sID="gen24344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12978"/><hi type="bold">5. Consider your ways--</hi>literally, "Set your heart" on your ways. The plural implies, Consider both what ye have done (actively, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.40">La 3:40</reference>) and what ye have suffered (passively) [Jerome]. Ponder earnestly whether ye have gained by seeking self at the sacrifice of God. <div eID="gen24344" type="x-p"/>
entries.250096be3ca05aad76d7c6eeb6b508ed61648d59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12979"/><div sID="gen24345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12979"/>6. Nothing has prospered with you while you neglected your duty to God. The punishment corresponds to the sin. They thought to escape poverty by not building, but keeping their money to themselves; God brought it on them for not building (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.7">Pr 13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">11:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Mt 6:33</reference>). Instead of cheating God, they had been only cheating themselves.<div eID="gen24345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye clothe ... but ... none warm--</hi>through insufficiency of clothing; as ye are unable through poverty from failure of your crops to purchase sufficient clothing. The verbs are infinitive, implying a continued state: "Ye have sown, and been bringing in but little; ye have been eating, but not to being satisfied; ye have been drinking, but not to being filled; ye have been putting on clothes, but not to being warmed" [Moore]. Careful consideration of God's dealings with us will indicate God's will regarding us. The events of life are the hieroglyphics in which God records His feelings towards us, the key to which is found in the Bible [Moore].<div eID="gen24346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wages ... put ... into a bag with holes--</hi>proverbial for labor and money spent profitlessly (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.10">Zec 8:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Is 55:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jr 2:13</reference>). Contrast, spiritually, the "bags that wax not old, the treasure in heaven that faileth not" (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.33">Lu 12:33</reference>). Through the high cost of necessaries, those who wrought for a day's wages parted with them at once, as if they had put them into a bag with holes. <div eID="gen24347" type="x-p"/>
entries.760fb51605dc5272a58eb6fd115e3a8e8cad9736: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12980"/><div sID="gen24348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12980"/><hi type="bold">8. Go up to the mountain--</hi>Moriah [Rosenmuller]; Lebanon [Henderson]. Rather, generally, the mountains around, now covered with wood, the growth of the long period of the captivity. So <reference osisRef="Neh.8.15">Ne 8:15</reference>, "Go forth unto the mount," that is, the neighboring hills [Maurer].<div eID="gen24348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wood--</hi>Haggai specifies this as being the first necessary; not to the exclusion of other materials. Stones also were doubtless needed. That the old walls were not standing, as the Hebrew interpreters quoted by Jerome state, or the new walls partly built, appears from <reference osisRef="Hag.2.18">Hag 2:18</reference>, where express mention is made of laying the foundations.<div eID="gen24349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified--</hi>I will be propitious to suppliants in it (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.30">1Ki 8:30</reference>), and shall receive the honor due to Me which has been withheld. In neglecting the temple, which is the mirror of My presence, ye dishonor Me [Calvin]; in its being built, ye shall glorify Me. <div eID="gen24350" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b7d208cace93204318991f2b98d743146d0a257: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12981"/><div sID="gen24351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12981"/><hi type="bold">9. Ye looked for much--</hi>literally, "looked" so as to turn your eyes "to much." The Hebrew infinitive here expresses continued looking. Ye hoped to have your store made "much" by neglecting the temple. The greater was your greediness, the more bitter your disappointment in being poorer than ever.<div eID="gen24351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it--</hi>even the little crop brought into your barns I dissipated. "I did blow upon," that is, I scattered and caused to perish with My mere breath, as scattered and blighted corn.<div eID="gen24352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine house ... his own house--</hi>in emphatic antithesis.<div eID="gen24353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye run--</hi>expressing the keenness of everyone of them in pursuing their own selfish interests. Compare "run," <reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Psa 119:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Pr 1:16</reference>, contrasted with their apathy about God's house. <div eID="gen24354" type="x-p"/>
entries.d34753af1a2f0e74e41b2a82b583f89e7c3c41f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12982"/><div sID="gen24355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12982"/><hi type="bold">10. heaven ... is stayed from dew--</hi>literally, "stays itself." Thus heaven or the sky is personified; implying that inanimate nature obeys Jehovah's will; and, shocked at His people's disobedience, withholds its goods from them (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.12">Jr 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen24355" type="x-p"/>
entries.d70fa5ee59e5627d96fcb4093fa412e004215c32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12983"/><div sID="gen24356" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12983"/><hi type="bold">11. I called--</hi>what the "heaven" and "earth," the second causes, were said to do (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.10">Hag 1:10</reference>), being the visible instruments, Jehovah, in this verse, the invisible first cause, declares to be His doing. He "calls for" famine, &c., as instruments of His wrath (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.1">2Ki 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.16">Psa 105:16</reference>). The contrast is striking between the prompt obedience of these material agencies, and the slothful disobedience of living men, His people.<div eID="gen24356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drought--</hi>Hebrew, Choreb, like in sound to Chareeb, "waste" (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.4">Hag 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>), said of God's house; implying the correspondence between the sin and its punishment. Ye have let My house be waste, and I will send on all that is yours a wasting drought. This would affect not merely the "corn," &c., but also "men" and "cattle," who must perish in the absence of the "corn," &c., lost by the drought.<div eID="gen24357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labour of the hands--</hi>all the fruits of lands, gardens, and vineyards, obtained by labor of the hands (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.33">De 28:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.46">Psa 78:46</reference>). <div eID="gen24358" type="x-p"/>
entries.c819c19d6ee4015ba0a07e8c875747449ba8474a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12984"/><div sID="gen24359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12984"/><hi type="bold">12. remnant of the people--</hi>all those who have returned from the exile (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.6">Zec 8:6</reference>).<div eID="gen24359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... God sent him--</hi>according to all that Jehovah had enjoined him to speak. But as it is not till <reference osisRef="Hag.1.14">Hag 1:14</reference> after Haggai's second message (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.13">Hag 1:13</reference>) that the people actually obeyed, Maurer translates here, "hearkened to the voice of the Lord," and instead of "as," "because the Lord had sent him." However, English Version rightly represents their purpose of obedience as obedience in God's eyes already, though not carried into effect till <reference osisRef="Hag.1.14">Hag 1:14</reference>. <div eID="gen24360" type="x-p"/>
entries.3edae830d002be75ee8f8932b5846936fa4e7af5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12985"/><div sID="gen24361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12985"/><hi type="bold">13. the Lord's messenger--</hi>so the priests (Mal 2:7) are called (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.4.14">Ga 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2Pe 1:21</reference>).<div eID="gen24361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord's message--</hi>by the Lord's authority and commission: on the Lord's embassage.<div eID="gen24362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am with you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>). On the people showing the mere disposition to obey, even before they actually set to work, God passes at once from the reproving tone to that of tenderness. He hastens as it were to forget their former unfaithfulness, and to assure them, when obedient, that He both is and will be with them: Hebrew, "I with you!" God's presence is the best of blessings, for it includes all others. This is the sure guarantee of their success no matter how many their foes might be (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.31">Ro 8:31</reference>). Nothing more inspirits men and rouses them from torpor, than, when relying on the promises of divine aid, they have a sure hope of a successful issue [Calvin]. <div eID="gen24363" type="x-p"/>
entries.292de2457dbfa77ede9ab386af3c4a531f38366e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12986"/><div sID="gen24364" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12986"/><hi type="bold">14. Lord stirred up the spirit of, &c.--</hi>God gave them alacrity and perseverance in the good work, though slothful in themselves. Every good impulse and revival of religion is the direct work of God by His Spirit.<div eID="gen24364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came and did work--</hi>collected the wood and stones and other materials (compare <reference osisRef="Hag.1.8">Hag 1:8</reference>) for the work. Not actually built or "laid the (secondary) foundations" of the temple, for this was not done till three months after, namely, the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.18">Hag 2:18</reference>) [Grotius]. <div eID="gen24365" type="x-p"/>
entries.eaca6987ee4f4db7dfc2b4b0e30c82cd2eb16830: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12987"/><div sID="gen24366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12987"/><hi type="bold">15. four and twentieth day--</hi>twenty-three days after the first message of Haggai (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag 1:1</reference>). <chapter eID="Hag.1"/>

entries.937d03c4bf150def5e01839d1b37c04958982c04: <div eID="gen35341" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35342" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35343" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35343" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35342" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35344" type="x-p"/> The prophet reproves the people, and particularly their ruler and high priest, for negligence and delay in rebuilding the temple; and tells them that their neglect was the cause of their having been visited with unfruitful seasons, and other marks of the Divine displeasure, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.1-Hag.1.11">Hag 1:1-11</reference>. He encourages them to set about the work, and on their doing so, promises that God will be with them, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.12-Hag.1.15">Hag 1:12-15</reference>. <div eID="gen35344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35345" type="x-p"/> We know nothing of the parentage of Haggai. He was probably born in Babylon during the captivity, and appears to have been the first prophet sent to the Jews after their return to their own land. He was sent particularly to encourage the Jews to proceed with the building of the temple, which had been interrupted for about fourteen years. Cyrus, who had published an edict empowering the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild their city and temple, revoked this edict in the second year of his reign, through the evil advice of his courtiers and other enemies of the Jews. After his death Cambyses renewed the prohibition, but after the death of Cambyses, Darius, the son of Hystaspes, renewed the permission; and Haggai was sent to encourage his countrymen to proceed with the work. Darius came to the throne about the year b.c. 521, and published his edict of permission for the Jews to rebuild the city and temple in the second year of his reign, which was the sixteenth of their return from Babylon. <div eID="gen35345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35346" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35347" type="x-p"/> In the sixth month - Called Elul by the Hebrews. It was the sixth month of the ecclesiastical year, and the last of the civil year, and answered to a part of our September. <div eID="gen35347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35348" type="x-p"/> Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel - Who was son of Jeconiah, king of Judah, and of the family of David, and exercised the post of a governor among the people, but not over them, for both he and they were under the Persian government; but they were permitted to have Zerubbabel for their own governor, and Joshua for their high priest; and these regulated all matters relative to their peculiar political and ecclesiastical government. But it appears from Ezra, <reference osisRef="Ezr.5.3">Ezr 5:3</reference>, that Tatnai, the governor on this side the river, had them under his cognizance. None of their own governors was absolute. The Persians permitted them to live under their own laws and civil regulations; but they always considered them as a colony, over which they had a continual superintendence. <div eID="gen35348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35349" type="x-p"/> Joshua the son of Josedech - And son of Seraiah, who was high priest in the time of Zedekiah, and was carried into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.15">1Chr 6:15</reference>. But Seraiah was slain at Riblah, by order of Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18-2Kgs.25.21">2Kgs 25:18-21</reference>.
entries.74f108d738db9b3f04f455dac93736fc79a7d3b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35350" type="x-p"/> The time is not come - They thought that the seventy years spoken of by Jeremiah were not yet completed, and it would be useless to attempt to rebuild until that period had arrived. But Abp. Usher has shown that from the commencement of the last siege of Jerusalem unto this time, precisely sixty-nine years had been completed.
entries.b7fcdc7fd6f61ee2e42ce8823931f2ffc7771aaa: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35351" type="x-p"/> Is it time for you - If the time be not come to rebuild the temple, it cannot be come for you to build yourselves comfortable houses: but ye are rebuilding your houses; why then do ye not rebuild the house of the Lord? The foundation of the temple had been laid fourteen years before, and some considerable progress made in the building; and it had been lying waste in that unfinished state to the present time.
entries.e98c68437345784d919b430e8612c4d4aeef09f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35352" type="x-p"/> Consider your ways - Is it fit that you should be building yourselves elegant houses, and neglect a place for the worship of that God who has restored you from captivity?
entries.0a83d90003d77a4779a405e5548d7d519dd99ab9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35353" type="x-p"/> Ye have sown much - God will not bless you in any labor of your hands, unless you rebuild his temple and restore his worship. This verse contains a series of proverbs, no less than five in the compass of a few lines.
entries.caddbe0fbbbf286fde454c913c9e09808318e381: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35354" type="x-p"/> Go up to the mountain, and bring wood - Go to Lebanon, and get timber. In the second year of the return from the captivity, they had procured cedar trees from Lebanon, and brought them to Joppa, and had hired masons and carpenters from the Tyrians and Sidonians; but that labor had been nearly lost by the long suspension of the building. <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.7">Ezr 3:7</reference>.
entries.17a00ceca466c0ed199e985c8144ea29da5a4b09: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35355" type="x-p"/> Ye looked for much - Ye made great pretensions at first; but they are come to nothing. Ye did a little in the beginning; but so scantily and unwillingly that I could not but reject it. <div eID="gen35355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35356" type="x-p"/> Ye run every man unto his own house - To rebuild and adorn it; and God's house is neglected!
entries.e1b0afa864cb68a9f92655d339daab23e459b595: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35357" type="x-p"/> Therefore the heaven over you is stayed from dew - It appears from the following verse that God had sent a drought upon the land, which threatened them with scarcity and famine.
entries.681689499296eba2c07ea7696ff4d06ad49303cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35358" type="x-p"/> Then Zerubbabel - The threatening of Haggai had its proper effect. - The civil governor, the high priest, and the whole of the people, united together to do the work. When the authority of God is acknowledged, his words will be carefully obeyed.
entries.c21146d8995c14bb9ae3ffc32d5b024bf1df44ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35359" type="x-p"/> Then spake Haggai - He was the Lord's messenger, and he came with the Lord's message, and consequently he came with authority. He is called מלאך יהוה malach Yehovah, the angel of Jehovah, just as the pastors of the seven Asiatic churches are called Angels of the Churches, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.2">Rev 1:2</reference>. <div eID="gen35359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35360" type="x-p"/> I am with you, saith the Lord - Here was high encouragement. What may not a man do when God is his helper?
entries.063314576352f29210ac3212889436f79fc1e3f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35361" type="x-p"/> And the Lord stirred up the spirit - It is not only necessary that the judgment should be enlightened, but the soul must be invigorated by the Spirit of God, before any good work can be effectually done.
entries.8a8c587f03fb26043cdd3c38c7240af1fa4e9b2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen35361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35362" type="x-p"/> In the four and twentieth day - Haggai received his commission on the first day of this month and by the twenty-fourth day he had so completely succeeded that he had the satisfaction to see the whole people engaged heartily in the Lord's work; they left their own houses to build that of the Lord. Here was a faithful reprover, and he found obedient ears; and the Lord's work was done, for the people had a mind to work.  <chapter eID="Hag.1"/> <div eID="gen35362" type="x-p"/>

entries.3064f476b98b317b485716ad3029bf42bf294616: <div eID="gen16735" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-ms">Haggai</title> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16736" type="x-p"/> Person of the Prophet. - We have no further information concerning <hi type="italic">Haggai</hi> (<hi type="italic">Chaggai</hi>, i.e., the festal one, formed from <hi type="italic">châg</hi>, with the adjective termination ai: cf. Ewald, 164, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, and 273, <hi type="italic">e</hi>; lxx Ἀγγαῖος, Vulg. <hi type="italic">Aggaeus</hi>) than that obtained from the headings to his prophetic addresses (Hag 1:1; Hag 2:1, Hag 2:10, Hag 2:20), and confirmed by Ezr 5:1, - namely, that he commenced his prophesying in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, and by means of his prophecies caused the work of building the temple, which had been suspended in consequence of the machinations of the <hi type="italic">Cuthaeans</hi> (Samaritans), to be resumed, and in common with the prophet Zechariah, who commenced his labours two months later, ensured the continuance of that work. The extra-biblical accounts of the circumstances of his life have no evidence at all to support them. This is the case, for example, with the statement of Ps. Dorotheus and Ps. Epiphanius, that Haggai came from Babylon to Jerusalem when quite a young men, and that he survived the rebuilding of the temple, and was buried in honour near the burial-place of the priests, to say nothing of the strange opinion which was tolerably general in the times of Jerome and Cyril of Alexandria, and which arose from a misinterpretation of the word מלאך in Hag 1:13, viz., that Haggai was an angel who appeared in human shape. And Ewald’s conjecture, that Haggai had seen the temple of Solomon, cannot be inferred from Hag 2:3. In that case he would have been about eighty years old when he commenced his labours as a prophet. 2. The Book of Haggai contains four words of God uttered by the prophet in the second year of the reign of Darius Hystaspes, which had for their object the furtherance of the building of the temple, and in all probability simply reproduce the leading thought of His oral addresses. In the first prophecy, delivered on the new moon’s day of the sixth month of the year named (Hag 1:1-15), the condemns the indifference of the people concerning the building of the temple, and represents the failure of the crops and the curse under which the people were suffering as a divine punishment for the neglect of that work. In consequence of this admonition the building was resumed. The three following prophecies in ch. 2 encourage the people to continue the work they have begun. The second, which was delivered only twenty-four days after the first (Hag 2:1-9), consoles those who are desponding on account of the poverty of the new building, by promising that the Lord will keep the covenant promise made to His people when they came out of Egypt, and by shaking the whole world and all the heathen, will give the new temple even greater glory than that of Solomon had. The last two words of God were delivered to the people on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month of the same year. They predict in the first place the cessation of the previous curse, and the return of the blessings of nature promised to the church which had remained faithful to the covenant (Hag 2:10-19); and in the second place, the preservation of the throne of Israel, represented in the person and attitude of Zerubbabel, among the tempests which will burst upon the kingdoms of this world, and destroy their might and durability (Hag 2:20-23). <div eID="gen16736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16737" type="x-p"/> In order to understand clearly the meaning of these prophecies and promises in relation to the development of the Old Testament kingdom of God, we must look at the historical circumstances under which Haggai was called by God to labour as a prophet. Haggai was the first prophet who rose up after the exile in the midst of the congregation of Judah that had returned from Babylon, to proclaim to it the will and saving purposes of its God. Between him and Zephaniah there lay the seventy years’ exile, and the labours of the great prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. What all the earlier prophets had foretold, and Jeremiah especially, in a comprehensive and most impressive manner - namely, that the Lord would thrust out Judah also among the heathen, on account of its obstinate idolatry and resistance to the commandments of God, and would cause it to be enslaved by them - had been fulfilled. As the ten tribes had been carried away by the Assyrians long before, so had the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem been also carried into exile by the Chaldaeans through Nebuchadnezzar. The Lord had now banished all His people from before His face, and sent them away among the heathen, but He had not cast them off entirely and for ever. He had indeed suspended His covenant with Israel, but He had not entirely abolished it. Even to the people pining in exile He had not only renewed the ancient promises through the prophet Ezekiel, after the dissolution of the kingdom of Judah and the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, viz., that He would restore the nation to favour again, when it should come to the knowledge of its grievous sins, and turn to Him with penitence, and that He would redeem it from exile, lead it back to its own land, and exalt it to great glory; but He had also caused the might and duration of the kingdoms of the world to be proclaimed through Daniel, and their eventual overthrow through the kingdom of God from heaven. The seventy years, during which the land of Judah was to lie waste and the nation to serve Babel (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jer 25:11</reference>), had now passed away. The Babylonian empire had fallen, and Koresh (Cyrus), the founder of the Persian empire, had given the Jews permission to return to their own land in the first year of his sole dominion, and had commanded that the temple of Jehovah in Jerusalem should be rebuilt. In consequence of this, a considerable number of the captives of Judah and Benjamin, viz., 42,360 freemen, with 7337 men-servants and maid-servants, led by Zerubbabel prince of Judah, a descendant of David, who was appointed governor in Judah, and by the high priest Joshua, had returned to their homes (Ezr 1:1-11 and 2). Having arrived there, they had restored Jehovah’s altar of burnt-offering in the seventh month of the year, and re-established the sacrificial worship prescribed in the law. They had also so far made preparations for the rebuilding of the temple, that even in the second month of the second year after their return they were able solemnly to lay the foundation for the new temple (Ezr 3:1-13). <div eID="gen16737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16738" type="x-p"/> They had hardly commenced building, however, when the Samaritans came with a request that they might take part in the building of the temple, because they also sought the God of the Jews. Now, when the chiefs of Judah refused to grant them this request, as being a mixed people, composed of the heathen colonists who had been transplanted into the kingdom of the ten tribes and a few Israelites who were left behind in the land, whilst their worship of God was greatly distorted by heathenism (see at 2 Kings 17:24-41), they endeavoured to disturb the work already begun, and to prevent its continuation and completion. They made the hands of the people of Judah idle, as we read in Ezr 4:4-5, frightening them while building, and hiring counsellors against them to frustrate their design, the whole of the still remaining time of Cyrus, and even till the reign of king Darius of Persia, so that the work at the house of God at Jerusalem ceased and was suspended till the second year of the reign of this king (Ezr 4:24). But even if these machinations of the adversaries of Judah furnished the outward occasion for the interruption and suspension of the work they had begun, we must not seek for the sole and sufficient reason for the breaking off of the work in these alone. Nothing is recorded of any revocation of the edict issued by Cyrus during his reign; and even if the letter to Artachsata given in Ezr 4:7. referred, as is generally assumed, to the building of the temple, and the reply of this king, which prohibited the continuation of the building, was issued by <hi type="italic">Pseudo-Smerdis</hi>, this only took place under the second successor of Cyrus, twelve years after the laying of the foundation-stone of the temple.
